title: I will and I'm going to
subtitle: I'll do / I'm going to do
summary: Use will for a decision you make as you speak, and going to for a decision made earlier or for something the present situation shows is going to happen.

lesson.heading: A new decision: will
lesson.text: Sarah is talking to Helen. Sarah: 'Let's have a party.' Helen: 'That's a great idea. **We'll invite** lots of people.' We use **will** (We'll invite ...) to announce a new decision. The party is a new idea - the decision is made *now*.

examples.text: Let's have a party. That's a great idea. **We'll invite** lots of people.

lesson.heading: A decision already made: (be) going to
lesson.text: Later that day, Helen meets Max. Helen: 'Sarah and I have decided to have a party. **We're going to invite** lots of people.' We use **(be) going to** when we have already decided to do something. Helen had already decided to invite lots of people *before* she spoke to Max.

examples.text: Sarah and I have decided to have a party. **We're going to invite** lots of people.

left.label: will (deciding now)
examples: 'Gary has been trying to contact you.' 'Has he? OK, **I'll call** him.'
'Anna is in hospital.' 'Really? I didn't know. **I'll go** and visit her.'

right.label: going to (decided before)
examples: 'Gary has been trying to contact you.' 'Yes, I know. **I'm going to call** him.'
'Anna is in hospital.' 'Yes, I know. **I'm going to visit** her this evening.'

lesson.heading: Predicting the future: both are possible
lesson.text: We use both **will** and **going to** for future happenings and situations. Often you can say either.

examples.text: I think the weather **will be** nice later. or I think the weather **is going to be** nice later.
Those shoes are well-made. **They'll last** a long time. or **They're going to last** a long time.

lesson.heading: going to: the situation now shows it
lesson.text: When we say something **is going to** happen, we believe this because of the situation *now*. What is happening now shows that something is going to happen in the future.

examples.text: Look at those black clouds. **It's going to rain.** (we can see that it is going to rain - the black clouds are in the sky now)

lesson.heading: Evidence now, or what I know about a person?

left.label: going to (clear from the situation now)
examples: **We're going to be late.** The meeting starts in five minutes and it takes 15 minutes to get there. (it is clear now that we don't have enough time)

right.label: will (what I believe from experience)
examples: Jane **will be** late for the meeting. She's always late. (I believe this because I know what Jane is like)

lesson.text: If the words 'Yes, I know' or 'I've decided' fit before the sentence, use going to. If the idea only came to you as you spoke, use I'll.

exercises.prompt: Sarah: 'Let's have a party.' Helen: 'That's a great idea. ___ lots of people.'
exercises.explanation: The party is a new idea, so Helen announces a new decision with will.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I forgot my wallet. I don't have any money. *B:* Not to worry. ___ you some.
exercises.explanation: An offer decided at the moment of speaking: I'll lend you some.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Why are you filling that bucket with water? *B:* ___ the car.
exercises.explanation: The decision was made before (the bucket is already being filled): I'm going to wash the car.

pairs.left: Why don't you come to the party with us?

pairs.right: It looks as if it's going to fall down.
I think he's going to fall asleep.
I don't think it will fit in the room.

pairs.left: I haven't seen Ben for ages.

exercises.prompt: 'Gary has been trying to contact you.' 'Yes, I know. ___ him.'
exercises.explanation: 'Yes, I know' shows the decision was made earlier, so going to.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I've decided to paint this room. *B:* That's nice. What colour ___ it?
exercises.explanation: A asks about a decision that has already been made: What colour are you going to paint it?

exercises.statement: Look at those black clouds. It will rain.
exercises.explanation: It's going to rain. The clouds are evidence now, so we use going to.

exercises.prompt: Why does the speaker use will or going to?
categories: will: deciding now, or what I know about a person
going to: decided before, or clear from the situation now

items.text: Has he? OK, I'll call him.
Yes, I know. I'm going to call him.
Look at those black clouds. It's going to rain.
Jane will be late for the meeting. She's always late.
We're going to be late. The meeting starts in five minutes.
Really? I didn't know. I'll go and visit her.

exercises.prompt: *A:* This food doesn't taste very good, does it? *B:* No, it's horrible. ___ it.
answers: I am not going to finish
exercises.explanation: The situation now (horrible food) makes the intention clear: I'm not going to finish it.

exercises.statement: Jane will be late for the meeting. She's always late.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The speaker predicts from what they know about Jane, so will is right.

exercises.prompt: You: 'This camera is broken. ___ it away.' Your friend, who collects old cameras: 'Don't throw it away! ___ it.'
options: I'm going to throw / I'll have
I'll throw / I'm going to have
exercises.explanation: You had already decided (going to throw); your friend decides on the spot (I'll have it).

exercises.prompt: Amy has already offered to take Joe to the airport. Later Paul offers too. Joe says: 'Thanks, Paul, but ___ me.'
exercises.explanation: It was arranged earlier, so going to (or the present continuous), not will.
